newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl seeks answer for German woes in slimming cure.
newsitem.headline: Kohl seeks answer for German woes in slimming cure.

text.p: This year as never before, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl will be hoping a two-week slimming cure in the Alps gives him vision and strength to tackle a mountain of problems bigger than at any time in his 14-year tenure.
The gourmet chancellor traditionally uses his Easter holiday at an Austrian spa resort not just to lose weight but to set political priorities and often prepare a new initiative.

But this year he will have to search his soul to find the reasons why the two big reform projects he hoped would win his Christian Democrats the 1998 election -- pensions and taxes -- have fallen far short of expectations.

While the reforms have faltered or been ground down by lobby groups, the consensus-oriented social market system which they were supposed to preserve has begun to crumble, and Kohl has had to scramble to limit the damage.

Kohl's historic project of European monetary union has not only taken a back seat behind spiralling unemployment -- the project itself has looked increasingly doubtful as its linchpin, Germany, looks like failing to make the economic criteria.

"Taking stock now, you are led to the conclusion that the end of the reform drive has arrived...What other countries have achieved through painful structural reforms, Germany cannot manage," wrote the weekly newspaper Die Woche.

On Tuesday around 30,000 steel workers are expected to demonstrate in Frankfurt for fear that many of them will join the ranks of Germany's 12 percent unemployed in a predatory takeover or merger betwen steel giants Thyssen and Krupp.
Two weeks ago miners marched on Bonn's government quarter, angry about losing jobs as government subsidies are cut.
And thousands of construction workers stormed the site of the future parliament building in Berlin to protest against a slump that may make almost 100,000 of them unemployed this year.
The miners won extra cash, and the builders a pledge of a 25-billion-mark credit package to boost construction.
Kohl had apparently not seen the crises coming, just as he had not properly prepared the ground for his flagship projects.

Instead of restructuring the pay-as-you-go pensions system to cope with a huge increase in the proportion of older people in the next century, Kohl's party now looks content to merely raise contributions and cut payouts.

The "Grand Tax Reform" which was supposed to slash away a jungle of tax privileges, make the system more just and firms more competitive has finished up raising ordinary citizens' fears that the whole project is a tax increase in disguise.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have found it easy to play hard-to-get about negotiating with Kohl's coalition on a reform which they have the power to block through their majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament.

To many commentators, this shows Kohl has lost whatever chance he had to push through structural changes, above all by cutting the labour costs and welfare system which weigh the economy down at a time of harsh global competition.
Kohl, too, has had to throw his own political weight into uncomfortable day-to-day issues whose details he used to leave to others to hammer out while he kept a statesmanlike distance.
Worse still, the party he has controlled for decades with an iron hand has started to become restless and question his ability and determination to stay in power.
In February, Kohl said he would wait until after the European Union's reform summit in June to consider whether or not to stand for chancellor again in 1998.
The response from many in his party was that he should not dither but make up his mind over Easter and give the coalition a boost by announcing quickly that he would run again.

Kohl's aides, however, say the chancellor is much more likely to delay his decision for several months. Kohl knows, they say, that a new candidacy will not be enough if he cannot first show that he has policy answers to Germany's crisis.
